title: Editorial: The Centrality of Both Hyper- and Hypo-thalamocortical Connectivity in Psychosis.
abstract: Long-standing hypotheses about schizophrenia as a "dysconnection" syndrome are consistent with the idea that mental illness arises in part from brain circuit disruptions, with impairments in cognition and behavior occurring because of a failure of coordinated action across multiple brain regions. One such theory, put forth by Andreasen and colleagues, suggested that schizophrenia involves a disruption in the integration of cortical-striatal-thalamic-cerebellar circuits.<sup>1</sup> Anatomical work in primates has shown that the thalamus is topographically organized into parallel pathways connecting specific thalamic nuclei to different regions of cortex. The medial dorsal and anterior nuclei of the thalamus project to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), whereas the lateral nuclei project more to sensorimotor regions, with similar findings in functional brain connectivity studies in humans. A large body of evidence has shown reduced connectivity from bilateral thalamic regions, medial dorsal, and anterior nuclei in particular, to the bilateral dlPFC, dorsal anterior cingulate, parts of the striatum, and bilateral cerebellum in schizophrenia.<sup>2</sup> This is often coupled increased connectivity between the thalamus, lateral nuclei in particular, and motor, visual, and/or auditory sensory regions.<sup>2</sup>.
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
